DHT-02-02
Stiff person syndrome
C. Sommer/C3
Wu¨rzburg, Germany
Objective. To elucidate the pathophysiology of stiff person syndrome asso-
ciated with antibodies to amphiphysin.
Methods. Puriﬁed IgG from a patient with anti-amphiphysin positive stiff
person syndrome was injected intrathecally through indwelling catheters into
female Lewis rats. Rats were monitored for stiffness and spasms using video-
graphy and motor tests (rota-rod, footprints, grip strength), for explorative
behavior and anxiety (open ﬁeld, elevated plus maze), and for changes in spinal
synaptic functioin by electrophysiological recording of the H-reﬂex and of dorsal
root potentials.
Results. Intrathecal injection of IgG from a patient with anti-amphiphysin
associated stiff person syndrome induced symptoms of SPS in rats including
stiffness, spasms, decreased motor activity and reduced exploration in the open
ﬁeld and elevated plus maze suggesting increased anxiety- and fear-related
behavior. Depletion of the anti-amphiphysin speciﬁc antibodies from the patient
IgG by afﬁnity chromatography abolished these ﬁndings. Suppression of the H-
reﬂex by conditioning stimuli (up to 23% in control animals) was inhibited.
Compared to control animals dorsal root potentials were reduced in treated rats
after single and repetitive volleys to 43 and 51%, respectively, consistent with a
defect in GABAergic presynaptic inhibition.
Conclusion. Auto-antibodies to amphphysin can cause a disease of the central
nervous system by blocking synaptic inhibition.
DHT-02-03
Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome
F. Blaes/C3
/C3 Giessen, Germany
Objective. Childhood opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome (OMS) is a rare neu-
rological disease with the main symptoms opsoclonus, myoclonus and a severe
ataxia. Moreover, children have often a high irritability and developmental
disturbances. OMS can occur both without or with an associated neuroblastoma
as a paraneoplastic syndrome. Since the disease responds to immunosuppressants
and autoantibodies have been found in some patients, an autoimmune pathogen-
esis has been suspected.
Methods. We tested the sera of 30 patients with OMS (20 OMS with NB, 10
OMS without NB) for autoantibodies using immunohistochemistry, Western Blot
with 2D-gelelektrophoresis and mass spectrometry and ﬂow cytometry, the latter
to detect surface-binding autoantibodies.
Results. We identiﬁed to proteins which were recognised by more than one
OMS serum: alpha-enolase and KH-type splicing regulatory protein (KSRP). We
than tested all OMS sera on ELISA and Western Blot using recombinant alpha-
enolase. 6=30 OMS patients, but none of the controls were positive for auto-
antibodies against alpha-enolase. 4=30 patients had autoantibodies against KSRP .
Additionally we could show that almost all OMS patients had surface-binding
autoantibodies to a neuroblastoma surface epitope and 71% of the OMS patients
had autoantibodies to a surface epitope of cerebellar granular neurons. The
binding to neuroblastoma cells was associated with a proapoptotic and growth
inhibitory effect.
Conclusion. Taken together, we found that alpha-enolase and KSRP are
intracellular located autoantibodies in OMS, but the majority of the patients
have autoantibodies against surface epitopes of neuroblastoma and neuronal
cells. The functional effects of the autoantibodies support the idea of a humoral
immune-mediated disease.
Sunday, 3 June 2007 16.30–18.00 h Salon Petrini
